newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria ignores recession and pursues strong naira.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria ignores recession and pursues strong naira.

text.p: Nigeria's economy slumbers in recession and share prices have drifted lower due to falling profits but on Wednesday the central bank said it would keep pursuing a strong naira currency.

"It is part of a continuing process," commented a central bank official in the capital Abuja, who said the naira would exchange at 83.5 to the dollar at the weekly auction to banks, against 84.0 naira last week.

A strong and stable naira and apparent victory over inflation are held up as the prizes of the tight fiscal policy adopted by military ruler General Sani Abacha, who took power in economic and political chaos after a 1993 election was annulled.

But business is feeling the pinch of the government's aversion to spending the proceeds from crude oil exports at home since the funds are seen as a possible trigger for renewed inflation and a weaker naira.

"We don't really expect them to take it (the naira) below 83 quickly but they are sending a clear signal that they have no intention of letting the naira slip whatever the means or consequences," said one banker in the commercial capital Lagos.
After the naira lost six percent of its value in March, the purse strings were pulled as tight as they would go.
No 1997 capital expenditure budget has yet been approved and oil production joint-venture partners complain of cuts.
Meanwhile foreign reserves have topped $7 billion, up from $4.1 billion in December, which Finance Minister Anthony Ani linked to "public sector prudence and accountability".
Falling demand from banks for foreign currency, the yardstick used to decide the rate at which the central bank sells hard currency, has given the bank confidence to offer dollars for fewer naira.
"There are indications that the demand for forex may have fallen due to a corresponding fall in demand for goods and services," wrote Ijeoma Nwogwugwu in the independent Thisday newspaper.

Some of Nigeria's biggest companies have announced falling profits in recent months, dragging lower a stock exchange which had grown used to making steady gains. The all-share index has fallen 4.4 percent since late April.
"What we hope is that with the current strengthening of the naira, the government will see room for increased spending to reflate the economy," said one Lagos factory manager.

Business and the World Bank, looking for growth, were disappointed with Abacha's 1997 budget. This shied away from privatising inefficient utilities and kept a dual exchange rate which gives favoured branches of government and the military access to cheap foreign currency.

While foreign investors show increasing interest in other parts of Africa as potential emerging markets, there is little enthusiasm for giant Nigeria, with its history of political and economic turmoil and lack of accountability, analysts said.
The ruling generals have promised elections next year to restore civilian rule but have been criticised as insincere by local democracy campaigners and some Western countries.

"Assuming the political situation is under control, the economy could be kept in this low-level recessionary state for a long time, years even, while the military supports itself with oil money," said one Western economist.
